q: A small team builds a mobile app with live updates and offline use, and has no backend. What does Firebase look like?
why: Small team, real-time, offline and no backend to run are all signals that Firebase fits.

q: Staff need monthly reports joining customers, invoices and products. What do you choose?
o: A SQL database with a reporting tool
why: Relational data and SQL questions are a weak spot for Firestore, which has no joins in its standard edition and bills per read.

q: A working website only needs push. What is the sensible plan?
o: Add only Cloud Messaging; keep the backend
why: Adopt one piece: save tokens in the existing database and send from the existing server with the Admin SDK.

q: Which Firebase piece is hardest to leave?
why: Its data model, rules and live listeners are spread through the whole app.

q: Users want to search for words inside their notes. What is true for Firestore standard edition?
o: Use a search extension or the Enterprise edition
why: Full-text search is not in the standard edition; use an extension that copies data to a search service, or Enterprise edition text search.

q: A contract says data must stay in one country. What matters most?
o: Choosing the Firestore location at creation
why: The location is chosen once when you create the database and cannot be changed later.

q: Firestore can count, sum and average on the server, and these results update live in a listener.
why: Aggregation queries exist, but they do not work with live listeners or offline.

q: You can use Firebase Hosting alone, without Auth or Firestore.
why: Each Firebase product works on its own; Hosting is a common single piece and easy to leave.
